summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to the wealth tax assessment for the assessment year 1965 66 and that the Wealth Tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee interest due on accrual basis. The High Court dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, HELD: (1) The computation of the net wealth is not to be made in terms of the last day of the income tax tax. [310 E] (2) The computation is not to exceed the net wealth. The computation is to be made on the basis of the valuation date. The value of the asset is to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. There is no reason why the assets should be excluded from the net wealth on the basis that the assets are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assessee. [310 F G] (3) The computation has to be made by the Wealth Tax officer in accordance with section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act. The value is to be determined according to the principles laid down in the Act. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date, and the asset would produce if sold in open market on that date. [310 G H] (4) The computation under section 3 of Wealth Tax Act is not to determine the value of the assets of the assessee as on the valuation dates. The assets of the assesses are not confined only to cash. The value in the hands of the assessee is to be ascertained and it is not the value of any asset. [311 F G]

The respondent was a Time Keeper in the Beas river Beas river in the State of Orissa. He was a Time Supervisor in the Irrigation Project, Sundernagar. He was dismissed from service by the Central Administrative Tribunal, Chandigarh. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Tribunal had no power to modify the penalty award ed to the respondent when the findings recorded as to misconduct was supported by legal evidence. The High court further held that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the respondent was not a person likely to have off i cial dealings, with the respondent. The High, Court also held that the respondent had not been able to prove that the respondent committed any misconduct for which the penalty could lawfully be imposed. The High. Court also held the respondent guilty of the charges. The High 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was just a substitute to t he civil court and High Court. The Tribunal thus could exercise on ly such powers which the Civil Court or the High Court cou ld have exercised. The Tribunal, therefore, could exercise on the respondent 's own discretion in a suit or the High court cou ld have the jurisdiction to exercise all the powers whi ch the civil court could in a suit. [27G H] 2. The Tribunal is just a substitute for the disciplinary authority. The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with the punishment if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [27A B] 3. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to modify the punishment award ed to respondent when the finding of the Inquiry officer or the competentauthority is based on the evidence even if any of it is not based on any evidence. [27D] 4. The Tribunal could exercise on behalf of the respondent the power to modify or modify the penalty awarded to the respondent. [27E] 5. The Tribunal cannot exercise on behalf or on behalf of any other authority. The power of the Tribunal is not circumscribed by any limitation. It is not for the Court to substitute its own judgment to the same extent as it would be if the Tribunal were to act on the basis of the evidence adduced. [27F] 6. The Tribunal can exercise on behalf and on behalf of a Government servant if the conditions of the co n stitutional protection have been complied with, is not for any other purpose. [27H] 7. The Tribunal should not have acted on the basis on which the respondent was found guilty. [27C]

The appellants were charged with the offence of murder of one Malan, daughter of a deceased Malan. The prosecution case was that the deceased Malan was the wife of the deceased. She was the wife and the daughter of the deceased and the accused were the sons of the deceased, and the accused was the wife. The deceased Malan died on the spot. The deceased was taken to the hospital and was admitted to the hospital. The deceased died on the way to the hospital, and the doctor who conducted the post mortem examination found that the deceased was a homicidal one. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life under section 302 I.P..C. and also under section 302/34 I.P .C. The High Court, however, acquitted the accused. The State preferred an appeal to this Court against the acquittal of the accused. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 was not relied upon against the accused. [760 D] (2) The retracting judicial confession of the accused 5 was relied upon by the prosecution. The retracted Judicial confession of accused 6 was relied upon. The retractable judicial confession of appellant 5 was relied on by the prosecution in support of its case. The retreat was not relied on against the accused in this case. [761 D] (3) The retreat is not a substantive charge under section 302, I.P.,C. [762 D] (4) The retreating judicial confession of deceased Malan is not relied upon. [763 D] (5) The retoure of the retracting Judicial confession of the deceased Malu, a co accused in the murder of Malan, is not relied on. The retreated judicial confession of a co accused is not relied in the case against the accused, and the conviction of the accused for the murder of the deceased is not sustainable in law. [764 D] (6) The retransfer of the retracted judicial confessional statement of accused 5 to the effect that in pursuance of the conspiracy and in furtherance of their common intention they committed the murder of deceased Malu and accused 1 to 4 not guilty of charge No. 3 framed against them in respect of the murder of her husband and accused 1, 6 and 7, is not sustainable. [765 D] (7) The retribed judicial confession of co accused in respect of murder of Malu and in the absence of any evidence to show that the accused had committed the murder, the conviction of accused 5 is unsustainable in law. The retransferred judicial confession of coaccused 5 is not relied against the accused and the conviction and sentence awarded to him by the trial court under section 302 IPC is unsustainable in the law. [864 D]

The appellant was the sole executor of the will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, in favour of her husband. The appellant was the only son of the testator. The appellant had a subsisting interest in the properties in question. The appellant, who was the sole heir of the testator, claimed a declaration that the will was void and the appellant was entitled to dispose of them by a will. The trial court held that the will set up by the appellant was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmamma and the appellant had no right to dispose of it. The High Court, however, thought that the will did not prove that the will had been duly executed. The High court, however, did not agree with the appellant 's contention that the will in question was not proved. The High 'Court, however, took the view that the will showed that the testator at the relevant time was in a sound and disposing state of mind and that the will gave no effect to the will. The High, Court thought that the evidence adduced by the appellant to prove its execution was not satisfactory. Held, that the will could not be said to be proved to be a will within the meaning of section 80 of the Indian Evidence Act. The will was read out to the testatrix and she understood the nature and effect of the dispositions and put her signatures on it when she was in a well and disposing state. The will did not show that the testator was in a good and disposing state and that the testator had put his signatures on it. The will showed that it was a genuine document and the will was read over to the testatrix. The will also showed that the will contained the words "if a will is rational on the face of it and appears to be duly executed". The will was not proved and the will did no mention of the whole of the document. The will clearly showed that the signature of the testator was the signature of her testator. The will, therefore, did not prove the execution of the will.

The petitioners, who were lessees of a minor mineral, challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the (67 of 1957) of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the notification was in contravention of the provisions of section 15 of that Act and that the notification did not specify the area or the area of the area covered by a minor mineral and that the impugned notification was in violation of section 15. The petitioners also contended that the impugned Notification was in contravention with section 15 of Act and that section 15 was not applicable to the petitioners. The petitioners challenged the validity and the validity of the notification on the ground that section 15 of Gujarat Minor Mineral Act, 1966 was ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioners submitted that section 15 did not apply to the petitioners and that the notifications were in contravention of section 15 and that section 14 of the Act was ultra vires. The petitioners further contended that the notifications did not specify any area or the areas of the area in respect of which a Parwana could be issued and that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of section 15 as they were not the owners of the minor minerals. The petitioners ' contentions were that the impugned notifications were in violation of the provisions contained in section 15 of 1957 Act and that they were in contravention with the provisions of the Act and that, therefore, the impugned notification in question was in contravention Of section 15 of 1967 Act. The petitioners opposed the validity of these notifications and contended that section 15 had no application to the petitioners as the impugned notification did not contain any provision for the grant of a concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and the Rules. The petitioners relied on the decision of this Court in the case of [M.P.V. Sundararamier & Ors. vs State of Andhra Pradesh & Ors.] [1985] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 942. The petitioners urged that section 15 could not be said to be violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification in the present case was in contravention and was in contravention thereof. [411D] 2. The impugned notifications were not in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution and were therefore liable to be struck down. [411E] 3. The appellant was charged under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 302/34 IPC. The High court acquitted the appellant. The High 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: The High Court was not right in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of a single witness. The High Courts have not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of this solitary eye witness. The evidence of PW 4 in the first information report is true and it is not possible to adopt that course in this case where the testimony of the sole eye witness has been rejected with reference to the first accused who was on the same boat with the appellant. [711F G] The High Court has not considered the evidentiary value of the testimony of this solitary witness. The fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute the witnesses for the deceased was not considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence. But the fact that the witness has stated in the first informant 's first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical evidence. Besides, he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running ahead of the deceased. The High. Court has not given any consideration to the evidence of PW 5 in so far as he implicated the second accused and Tharnizharasan in the case of murder of the deceased, as the High Court has completely given a go by to this case. [712F G]

The appellant was the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff, who died on July 7, 1949. The respondents were the heirs and the legal representatives of Amarchand N, Shroff, who was the legal representatives. Amarchand N died on July 8, 1949, and the respondents were the legal representatives on the death of Amarchand. Amarchand died on July 1, 1950. The respondents filed a suit for the recovery of the amount due from them. The respondents contended that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by the heirs and other legal representatives of the deceased were liable to be assessed to income tax. The respondents also contended that the amounts were received by them after the death of the deceased and that they were liable to tax under section 24B. The respondents contested the suit on the ground that the amounts received by them were not liable to tax. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the amounts which had been received by the respondents were not liable for the tax assessed to income Tax. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The legal personality of a deceased assessee is extended for the duration of the entire previous year in the course of which he died and therefore the income received by him before his death and that received by him after his death, and that received after his death and therefore the respondents were liable to pay income tax. [707 E] (ii) The legal character of a deceased person is extended for a period of time to enable him to make an assessment of the total income of the deceased person and certain other consequences follow but in all the cases enumerated above the language used in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 24 B is restricted to the income received after the death. [709 E] (iii) The words "where the income is not so assessed" in section 24B are wide enough to include the legal personality of the deceased. The words " where the income is assessed" in the opening words of section 24A indicate that the legal personality is extended to the legal personality. [711 A B]

The appellant was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and in two of them also for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant of all the offences. The State then preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals for offences under ss. 52 and 471 of Indian Post Office act, 1898. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant was not in exclusive possession of the letters in question. The appellant had a better opportunity to get at postal articles it had to find affirmatively that the almirah was in the exclusive possession of him. The appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 136 of the Constitution. The High court was right in holding that though the locked almirah was not in the exclusive use of the appellant, the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be he who must be deemed to be in possession of the almirah and consequently of its contents including the registered letters in the name of the appellant. The appellant could not be said to have secreted the letters in his possession exclusively or even jointly with his father because he had the opportunity to get the keys of the almirahs in his possession. The appellant 's case was that the almirahs were in the exclusive knowledge of the appellant and that the almiraha contained a large numbers of articles belonging of the father and as such the appellant could not have any grievance. The appellant, therefore, could not be held to have secreting the letters in the possession of the appellant in his possession merely because he had a better chance to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilized the opportunity and was therefore in possession of a almirah.

The appellants were the Sarpanch of a Panchayat. The Panchayat was a body corporate and the Panchayat was constituted under the provisions of the Act. The Panchayat consisted of three members. The Sar-panch was not, therefore, a necessary party. The Sarwanch was not entitled to any such power. The Sar sanch was not required to be a party to any proceeding. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was guilty under section 302, I.P.,C. The appellant, a company, was appointed as a workman in the appellant company. The respondent was employed as a workman. The appellant was paid wages at the rate of Rs. 2/ per day. The appellant claimed that the award was not made in terms of the award and that the award did not amount to an illegal deduction from their wages. The appellant contended that the award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/- per day and in pursuance of the said award the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents, one that the award should be set aside and the award should not be set aside. The respondents contended that the appellant was not entitled to the award as the award did amount to an unfair labour practice. The respondents, however, contended that the awards were not binding on the appellant and that the appellant had not been given any opportunity of being heard. The respondents contested the claim. The appellant urged that section 15 of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did no amount to an award. The respondents also contended that the claims of the respondents were barred by limitation. The respondents urged that section 2(vi) of the Act did not apply to the case and that the claims were barred by time. The respondents relied on the decision of the Patna High Court in M/s. [M. C. A. No. 1 of 1963 decided on March 20, 1964. The appellant 's contention was that the award could not be said to amount to an agreement between the parties and that the respondents were not entitled to claim wages under the award. Held, that the award must be set aside on the ground that it was not made by the appellant. The award did not purport to be an award in terms of section 2(i) of the , nor did it amount to an arbitration award. The award does not purport to refer to the terms of the contract of employment. The award was not an award in the sense that it was an award in a sense of the law of the land. The award could not, therefore, be said to be an illegal award. The awards were not made by an industrial tribunal. The award merely stated that the terms prescribed by an award in law and in substance, constitute a fresh contract between the parties. The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charged with having committed an offence under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code, and under section 409 of the Indian penal Code, for having committed an act of criminal misappropriation of Rs. 1,000. The trial Magistrate convicted him under section 465 and 409 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but the High Court acquitted him. The State appealed to the Supreme Court. HELD : The appellant was not guilty of any offence under section 409, because, he was charged with an offence under the section, and no sanction was required for a prosecution under that section. The appellant was charged with the offence under section 477 A of the Indian IPC, and the charge under section 409 was therefore, not established. [1305 B] The appellant was prosecuted under section 409. The charge under section 477A was therefore, clearly one of misappropriation of funds. The appellant could not, therefore, be convicted under section 409 because, he had been charged with an act of misappropriation of Rs, 1,000 and not a criminal misappropriation. The appellant had been charged under section 409 for having committed a criminal misappropriation of a sum of Rs. 2,000 and had been charged for having committed criminal misappropriation of the sum of Rs, 2,000. [1306 C] The appellant had not been charged with any offence under the Act. The charge was therefore, rightly held to be proved. [1307 F] The appellant could be convicted under the section. [1308 C] The fact that the charge was one of misappropriation by a public servant, whether sanction is required under section 197(1) will depend upon the facts of each case. The appellant cannot be convicted under that section, because, the charge under the section is not one of misappropriation. [1300 F] The fact of the appellant being charged with an alleged offence under section 471 A of the Penal Code, does not make him guilty of any other offence. [1301 F] The charge under the sections is therefore, not one of criminal misappropriation. [1311 F]

The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the loss could not be set off against the business profits made in the erstwhile State of Travancore. The High Court, on a reference, held that the appellant was not entitled to the deduction of the losses under section 32(1) and the second proviso to section 34(1) Of the Indian Income. tax Act, and that, in any case, the loss could be set off only against the profits arising in an Indian State or in the latter case in any other Indian State or British India. The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, on the 8th June 1955, and was served with the grounds of detention. The grounds of detention were vague. The grounds were vague. It was contended that the grounds were vague and not in public interest. Held, that the grounds of the detention were vague and the grounds were not vague. The order of detention was not a mere formality and the order was not a nullity. The order was not an empty formality. The order could not be said to be a mere formality. The mere fact that the grounds furnished were vague would not be sufficient to vitiate the order. The order must be held to be a nullity. In the present case the grounds of non disclosure were vague. In the instant case the grounds were irrelevant and the grounds of invalid detention were vague, and the order of detention could not be held to have been made without any real application of mind. The order did not disclose the grounds of vague and not vague. In view of the fact that the appellant had exercised his right to ask for particulars, at the time when the grounds were furnished, the order was invalid. The order made by the Government of Bombay on the 8. June 1955 was not a speaking order. The grounds could not be considered as vague. The fact that the order was made without any representation of mind by the detaining authority was not a sufficient ground for the detention. The order, therefore, was not a non compliance with the provisions of section 3(2) of the Act. The order is not a mere procedural order. The right to be furnished is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) which is a substantive right. The right of the detenue to be furnished under article 22 (6) is subject to limitation under article 19(6) of the Constitution. The right is subject to reasonable restrictions. The right under article 22 is subject to a limitation under article 21. The right conferred by article 22 is not subject to any limitation under article 14. The right not to be furnished, as a matter of right, is subject to any limitations under article 19. The right in the present case was not a procedural right. The order does not disclose any particulars of the grounds of grounds of detention, nor is it a mere formality, and the mere fact that there was no representation of the grounds cannot be a ground for the order. It is not necessary to disclose the grounds. The order has to be communicated to the detenue at the time of the order. If the detenue does not exercise his right to make a representation, the order is not void. The order cannot be said to have been passed without any representation. The order in question was not a notice to the detenue. The order merely disclosed the grounds of his detention. The fact of the grounds not being communicated to the detenu at the time the grounds were supplied does not make the order a nullity. It is only the satisfaction of the detaining authority that is required. The order would be invalid. The State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya, ; , referred to.

The appellant was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. The Army Ordnation Corps Training Centre was abolished and the appellant was removed from service. The appellant was removed by the Central Government under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The appellant challenged the order of removal from service on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the order of dismissal was ultra vires the Army Rules and (2) that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. Held, that the order was ultra vires and that the action of the appellant was without any basis. The order was not ultra vires the Act and was not ultra. The order of removal was not without jurisdiction. The order did not amount to a valid rule. The order could not be said to be invalid merely because the appellant was not a party to the proceedings. The order passed by the Central Govt. was not without authority. The order, therefore, was not without any authority and was not invalid. The order is not without authority and is not invalid. It is not invalid for the reason that the Central Govt., after due consideration of the reports, had come to the conclusion that the appellant was guilty of misconduct. The order does not amount to an order of dismissal. The order must be set aside. The order made by the Central Govern ment is not without jurisdiction and is not vitiated by any error of law. The order cannot be said to have been made without jurisdiction. It is a nullity. The order in question was not without the authority of law. It was not a nullity. It was a nullity. In the instant case the order was not without a proper application of mind. The order had been made without any authority, and was not without proper application of the rules. The order therefore was not without legal authority.

The appellants were prosecuted for offences under section 31(1) read with section 33(1) of the . The Chief Presidency Magistrate acquitted all the accused including the appellants and held that the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, and that the proceedings had been closed. The appellants appealed to the High Court and the High Court held that the Conciliation Officer was bound to make his report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceedings and that the conciliation proceeding could not be said to be pending when Louis Pereira was dismissed. Held, that the conciliation was not completed when the report under section 12(6) was made by the Conciliation Officer but when that report was received by the appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings could be prolonged much beyond what was contemplated by the Act and the termination would depend upon what was contemplated under the Act and not what was contemplated. The conciliation proceeding could be prolonged only when the report was received and the conciliation proceedings were closed. The conciliation was not concluded when the report of the Conciliation Officer could be said to have been made by the appropriate government. The conciliation Proceedings could be prolonged even beyond what was envisaged by the Act. The conciliation could be prolonged beyond what was intended by the Act, and the conciliation proceeding was pending at the time when the report had been received by the Conciliation officer. The conciliation machinery could not be terminated when the report is received by the Government. The proceedings could not be concluded when the reports were not closed but were carried on as they were in the present case or if the Conciliation Officer delays the submission of his report his action (1) was not concluded within the meaning of section 12(1) and (2) the conciliation proceedings could not terminate when the report became final. The conciliation action could not be continued when the report made by the conciliation officer was received by him.

The appellant firm was a partnership firm carrying on business in the name of the firm. The firm was dissolved on March 31, 1977. The firm continued to be a partnership firm. The partnership firm was dissolved and the firm was dissolved. The firm filed a suit for a declaration that the cinema licence dated July 22, 1969 issued by the District Magistrate was void and inoperative and that the firm was not entitled to claim a renewal of the licence. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the renewal of the cinema licence was not in the name and that the licence was not transferable. The High court, in appeal, held that the licence could not be said to have been granted to the firm and that the renewal was not in any way invalid. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licence in respect of the Apsara Theatre was granted by the District and Sessions Judge, Jammu, and that the District Magistrate had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The licence in respect thereof was granted by District Magistrate in the sole name of Ved Gupta and in all the relevant columns of the document of licence, Ved Gupta had been shown as the licensee and there is no mention at all of the firm or its partners. An application filed by Shri Ved Gupta for a declaration under section 6 of the Act was not maintainable. [581 D] The licence in the instant case was granted by a District Magistrate in his individual capacity or as representing the partnership. The licence in question was granted by his District Magistrate in respect of a cinema theatre. The licence was granted by him in the sole names of Ved Gupta, and in all other columns of the documents of licence, the licence was granted to the District Magistrate. The licence therefore was granted by that District Magistrate. [582 E F] The licence was not a transferable one. The licence could not have been transferred to the firm. [583 E F] In the instant case, the licence in the name was granted by one of the partners of the firm who wanted to run the Theatre without a licence in contravention of the provisions of the Act and the Rules. The licence, in the instant ease, was granted by another person. The licence granted by the district Magistrate was valid. [584 E F]

The respondent, a Custodian of Evacuee Property, filed a suit for a declaration that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 12 of the (XXXI of 1950) and for a declaration of his right to possession of the properties. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court in appeal reversed the decree of the trial court. The High Court held that section 12 of Act XXXI of 1950 did not apply to properties of the evacuee and that the properties of the respondent were evacuee property and under section 8(1) of the Act, they became the property of the evacuee by reason of the sale in favour of the appellants. The High 'Court further held that section 10 of the Act did not apply and that the respondent had no power to cancel the lease in favour of his father. The High court, however, held that section 8(i) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, did not apply, and that the notice was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section. The High, Court, however, in appeal, held that the respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice and that the property in question had become the property of evacuee by reason only of the sale of the property in favour of a third party. On appeal by the State, Held, that the respondent could not be said to have been acting within his powers in issuing the notices under section 12. The respondent was acting in excess of his powers under section 12 and was therefore not entitled to cancel the notice. The respondent could not, therefore, be said to be acting within his jurisdiction in issuing the said notice. The notice was not ultra vires the power of the Custodian to cancel the agreement to sell the mills and the factory to them which was one of the matters contained in Exhibit A. The respondent had no authority under section 12 to cancel the said lease in favour. The respondent, therefore, was acting within the authority of the Custodian in issuing the lease in his favour.

The High court, however, held that the expression "Government of the corresponding State" used in article 295(2) of the Constitution was not a "Government of a corresponding State" within the meaning of article 295(1) of the constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The respondent was entitled to claim the benefit of the provisions of article 295 (2) of that Constitution. The Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, was passed to provide for the better regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops in the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make bye laws for the regulation of the business and the conditions of trading therein. The Act provided for the better regulating the buying and selling and selling of such agricultural produce and for that matter to establish markets, and make bye law for the regulation and control of the business. The Act did not provide for the proper administration of the market and the rules made thereunder. The Act, however, provided that no licence for the purchase or sale of such commercial crops shall be granted or renewed in respect of any place situated within such distance from the market as may from time to time be fixed by the State Government. The Act also provided for the regulation or control of the purchase and sale of such agricultural crops. The Act further provided that no person shall enter into any contract for the purchase of any commercial crop in quantities not exceeding those prescribed by the rules made under the Act. The appellants challenged the validity of the Act and Rules framed thereunder. They contended that the Act and rules framed thereunder were not ultra vires the Act and that the Act was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the Act did not offend article 14 of Constitution. The Act and the Rules framed thereunder were valid. The Act does not offend article 19 of the Constitution because the Act does not provide for any particular payment of tax. The petitioners, who were manufacturers of cotton and cotton, challenged the levy of excise duty on the ground that the assessable value of the processed fabric was Rs.20 and not Rs.20. The Central Excise and Gold (Control) Act, 1947, was enacted with a view to provide for the levy of duties of excise on the manufacture of cotton and for the manufacture of the goods. The petitioners contended that the assessable values of the processed fabrics were Rs.20, and not Rs,20. The petitioners also contended that the value of the grey cloth in the hands of processor plus the value of job work done plus the manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses, which would include the value of grey yarn in the hands and the processor plus his profit. The Central Government, however, rejected the contention of the petitioners. The petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the levy of the excise duty on ground that the value was not Rs. 20 but Rs.20 as the value of a grey machinery in the hands or processor plus a value of the job work done minus the manufacturing profit. The petitioners 's writ petitions were dismissed by the High Court. In the special leave petitions to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the assessablevalue of the processed goods would be the value of Rs.20 but the manufacturing profit would be the correct as sessable value. Dismissing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessable value of processed fabric would be the market value of the goods in the hands, or processor. The assessable values would be the valuation of the processed product and excise duty would be charged to the processor on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, would include only the price or deemed price at which the processed fabric would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit, and manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. [ 345B C] 2. The assessablevalue of processed fabric will be the value for the processed fabric and excise duty will be charged to that processor on the basis of the price at the factory gate. [ 345C] 3. The assessable Value of processed fabric shall be the value calculated on the basis as per the formula for the purpose of the levy of duty of excise. [ 345D]

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, which was a clerk. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by the Panchayat Samitis to the effect that the appellant should be absorbed as a Head clerk on an adhoc basis. The appellant was confirmed in the post in course on April 1, 1975. On April 1,1975 the appellant was appointed temporarily as Head Clerk on a permanent basis. On April l, 1975 the appellant, was confirmed in his post in course. On April 25, 1975, the appellant was promoted as Head Clerk. On April 28, 1975 he was confirmed in service. On April 30, 1975 his services were regularised as a Head Cashier. On April 27, 1975 another resolution was passed to the effect, that the appellant would be absorbed as Head Clerk in the Government service on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayat. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court, challenging the validity of the Amending Act of 1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the Amending act, the appellant had become entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same conditions on which they were employed by the Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head Clerk being without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post of the Head Clerk. The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of land a part of the land allotted to them in the year 1949. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of allotment of land in the year 1952. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellants then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Custodian. The High court dismissed the petition holding that the order of cancellation of allotment was invalid. The appellants moved the High court under article 226. The High ' Court held that the order was invalid. Held, that the order passed by the Custodian was invalid. It was not correct to say that section 19(1) of the Act was completely in conflict with section 10 of the in so far as the question of cancellation of the allotment was concerned. The order was invalid because the order was not passed under section 12(1) and the order was therefore invalid. The order of the High Court was therefore valid. The order passed by it was not invalid. The Custodian was not competent to cancel the allotment. The order did not affect the rights of the appellants. The order could not be said to be invalid merely because the order of transfer was not passed in the manner prescribed by section 12(2) of the 1954 Act. The order must be set aside. The order is set aside. It is open to the Custodian to cancel the allotments and to revise the order of allotments. The order does not affect the right of the appellants to have their allotments cancelled. The order cannot be said to have been passed under section 10 of 1952 Act. The Custodian had no power to cancel the order of allot ing the land. The order in question was therefore valid and the order of cancelling the allotment was invalid and the order could not therefore be challenged.

The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the levy of tax was invalid. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant companies that the provisions of the Municipalities Act and the Municipal Corporation Act were not incorporated into the Act of 1973 by its section 69(d) of the Act of 1961. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was incompetent to exercise the powers of the Municipality or the Municipal Council under section 127A of the Act. [864 F] The High Court has rightly held that the levy is invalid. The High Courts have held that the provisions in the Municipalities Act, and the Municipal Act are not incorporated into it. The Municipal Corporation Act, 1966, is a special Act and the provisions of section 133 of the Act are not in any way inconsistent with the provisions of any other law. [865 A] The Municipal Corporation of Indore vs M/s. M. P. Special Area Development Authority, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 970, followed.
